text:
Cupola

 A Cupola over your server. 

One native app for your entire self-hosted media stack, and the box it runs on. 
 19 services. iOS, Android, macOS. No cloud, no account, no middleman. 
 Install · Supported services · Security & privacy

 
 
 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 

 

---

 Why Cupola

Running a media stack means running a dozen web UIs. On a phone, most of them are
unusable, and none of them know about each other. Cupola is one app that knows
about all of them.

- The whole stack. Seerr, the arr family, four download clients,
 two media servers, and the infrastructure underneath: TrueNAS, Unraid, Dockge,
 Nginx Proxy Manager, each with its own screens.
- No Cupola server. No relay, no sign-up, and no telemetry of ours. The app
 speaks directly to the hosts you own, and credentials live in the device keychain.
 One exception, explained under Security & privacy:
 background search hands a request to the OS, API key included, so it ships off.
- Built for home labs. Self-signed certificates, services behind a reverse
 proxy, boxes that are asleep or out of reach: Cupola handles them as everyday
 states.
- It tells you what needs you. A stuck download, a disk with errors, an
 indexer that stopped watching for releases: Cupola says what happened and puts
 the fix on the same card.
- Phone first. Designed for the phone, then the tablet and the desktop window,
 with the same design on every platform.

---

 Install

 Just want to use it? iPhone and iPad install through TestFlight (or a sideloaded
 .ipa ); Android and macOS download from
 Releases .
 No toolchain needed. The App Store and Google Play come later.

 No server at hand? On the first screen, Explore a demo home opens an invented
 household with all nineteen services. It runs entirely inside the app: nothing is
 saved and nothing goes out to the network. Settings → Leave demo takes you back.

 Platform Status Get it 
 --- --- --- 
 iOS / iPadOS Supported, iOS 17+ TestFlight, or an unsigned .ipa from Releases 
 Android Supported, Android 7.0+ .apk from Releases, or Obtainium 
 macOS Supported, Apple silicon, macOS 12+ .dmg from Releases 
 Windows / Linux Built by CI, untested .zip / .tar.gz from Releases 
 Web Not a goal none 

 Coming from Seekarr? Cupola 1.0 is a new app , not an update. It installs
 beside Seekarr and starts empty: add your services again (same URLs, same API keys),
 check that they answer, then uninstall Seekarr. In Obtainium, the Seekarr entry may
 offer Cupola and then refuse it, because the app ID changed: remove that entry and add
 Cupola as a new app. Releases before 1.0.0 were published as Seekarr and cover fewer
 services than this page describes.

 
 iOS and iPadOS 
 

Open the TestFlight link on your iPhone or iPad, install Apple's
TestFlight app when it asks, then tap Install . TestFlight brings each new version
on its own. The public link has a limited number of places: if it says the beta is
full, try again after the next release.

To sideload instead, download cupola- .ipa from Releases and install it with
AltStore, SideStore or Sideloadly. The file is unsigned: your tool signs it with your
own Apple ID. With a free Apple ID the install lasts 7 days and has to be refreshed,
and the widgets may stay empty, because they share data through an App Group that a
re-signed copy may not get. TestFlight is the way we recommend.

 

 
 Android 
 

Download an .apk from Releases and install it. You may need to allow installs from
unknown sources for your browser or file manager.

- cupola- -arm64-v8a.apk is for 64-bit phones, which is nearly all of them,
 and less than half the size.
- cupola- .apk covers every device, older 32-bit phones included.

Both carry the same signature and version number, so a phone can move from one to the
other without uninstalling.

To get updates without checking this page, add this repository's URL to
 Obtainium : it installs the .apk from each new
release.

 

 
 macOS 
 

Download the .dmg , drag Cupola to /Applications , and launch it. The 1.0 build
runs on Apple silicon Macs only. The app is signed with a Developer ID and notarized
by Apple, so it opens like any other.

 

 
 Windows, Linux 
 

Both have a real runner with the desktop window. Each release carries a build made by
GitHub Actions: on Windows unzip it and run cupola.exe (the build is not signed, so
SmartScreen asks once); on Linux untar it and run cupola (it needs GTK 3 and
libsecret, present on most desktops). We have not run either ourselves, so a report
either way helps.

 

---

 Supported services

Configure only what you run: a service you have not set up stays out of the way.

Two columns say how far each integration goes:

- Control. How far Cupola goes today: full read and write, or mostly reading.
- Tested. Whether the integration has been exercised against a real, running
 instance . Every service also has unit tests, which is a separate thing. We fill
 this column in conservatively:
 ✅ verified end to end · ◐ partial , where the screens have read a real
 instance (or a faithful stand-in) but its actions have not been run against one ·
 ○ untested , written to the official API but never run against a live

features.title: Features
features.html:
Home: the evening at a glance

What arrived on your server, what airs or comes out next, what you were halfway through, and what needs you, on one page. Home is made of modules: keep the ones you want, in the order you want, and leave the rest out.

Discover: find something to watch

Trending this week, a calendar of what is coming, and every way in: genres, networks, studios, people, decades, moods and languages, plus the collections you have only part of. Type once and Seerr, Radarr, Sonarr, Jellyfin, Plex and Emby answer side by side, so "do I already have this?" takes one search.

Tap a poster and one page tells you the ratings, who is in it, where it stands on your server, and opens the trailer. Then act from that same page: add it to your library, send a request, pick a specific release yourself, or clear out something you no longer want.

Activity: what went wrong, and how to fix it

Needs you gathers what the stack cannot fix by itself: a download stuck for days, imports waiting for a decision, a disk reporting errors, an indexer that stopped watching for new releases. Each one says what happened, keeps the service's raw message one tap away, and offers the fix first: try another download, look for peers again, review the import, scrub the pool.

Downloads from all four clients sit in one list, moving first and stuck next. Open one to stop or resume it; on the desktop the table does it from the row. Requests and history are a tab away.

Stack: every service, with its own tabs

The Stack shows the whole lab in bands (media, downloads, streaming, the box itself) and says which services are clean and which need a look. Each service opens on its own Overview, with its own tabs: Radarr's library, calendar, queue and wanted list; qBittorrent's queue with filters, sorting, categories and tags; TrueNAS's full console.

  • Grab something automatically, or open the release list and choose it yourself
  • Flip monitoring, change quality profile, import files that landed in the wrong place
  • Delete, choosing whether the files go too and whether it may be added again
Outside the app: widgets and notifications

Home-screen widgets on iOS and Android: Coming up and Downloads for whoever runs the stack (Downloads also on the iPhone lock screen), Requests for a household member. Two notifications, both off until you turn them on in Settings → Notifications: Needs you, when something on the stack turns into a fault, and Ready to watch, when something you asked for arrives. The phone works them out itself, in the background, against your own services: there is no push server. How often that background run happens is up to the operating system.

At home and away

A connection can carry two addresses: the one it has at home and the one it has away from it (a reverse proxy, a tunnel, a VPN name). Cupola knocks on both and uses whichever answers, so the same app works on the sofa and on the train. A service that only exists at home says so and shows the last thing it knew.

Setting up a second phone takes one code: Settings → Security → Set up another device copies every connection across, encrypted, over your own Wi-Fi. To bring in someone from the household, Invite someone from Seerr gives them a link or a QR code that carries the server's address, never its API key.

For the whole household

Not everyone at home runs the stack. A household member signs in to Seerr with their own account (email, Jellyfin, Emby or Plex) and gets a simpler Cupola: Home, Discover and their requests, without the operator controls. Cupola never shows them a button the server would refuse.

Design and accessibility

Cupola is a native app, with no web view inside.

  • A black-and-white interface where colour carries meaning: green is done, amber is a fault, red is unreachable, blue is waiting
  • Light and dark themes, each designed on its own
  • Empty, failed and unconfigured screens explain what to do next
  • Text follows the system font size, up to the largest settings, without clipping
  • VoiceOver and TalkBack read each row as one sentence
  • Touch targets of at least 44 points
  • Designed for the phone first. On a tablet a title opens beside the list it came from; on the desktop the window gets a navigation rail, a command palette and an inspector
Searches that keep going in the background

Interactive search is slow because your indexers are slow. Tap Keep searching, put the phone away, and the answer is waiting in Activity when you come back.

On a phone that means the operating system runs the request for you, and to do that it writes the request down, API key included, until the search ends. Any app that searches in the background has to do this. So it ships off, and the switch in Settings → Background search explains the same trade-off. Cupola keeps the window narrow: a task expires after 11 minutes, finished records are cleared at every launch and the moment you switch the feature off, and on Android none of it is in a backup. On iOS one copy can ride along in a device backup: encrypt the backup, or use iCloud with Advanced Data Protection, and it is covered.

On desktop the question never arises. Nothing suspends the app, so a search just keeps running while Cupola is open.
